notes.meaning: Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur, Kinah, Dimonah, and Adadah lay in the dry southern region known as the Negeb. Kabzeel became famous as the home of Benaiah, one of King David's mightiest soldiers. By naming each town, God showed that His promise of land was concrete and touched real, everyday soil.

Kedesh, Hazor, and Ithnan were frontier towns along Judah's southern border with Edom. Little is known today about their exact ruins, but they were carefully marked out for Judah. God keeps track of every quiet corner of His people's inheritance.

Ziph, Telem, and Bealoth continued the list of southern border towns. Telem is likely the place called Telaim, where King Saul later gathered his army before fighting the Amalekites. God gave Judah this full territory so they would know what belonged to them and hold onto it.

Hazor-hadattah and Kerioth-hezron were settlements in the same dry southern region. Names like Hazor point back to cattle shelters, while Kerioth indicates a fortified town. Some writers think Kerioth gave Judas Iscariot his name, meaning the man from Kerioth.

These verses name nine more southern settlements, including the well-known town of Beersheba. Beersheba was famous as the home where Abraham and Jacob dug wells and lived for many years. God fulfilled His ancient promises to those patriarchs by giving this very ground to their great-grandchildren.

This group continues along the southern border of the tribe of Judah. Hormah was previously named Zephath, a place remembered for an early defeat when Israel wandered in the wilderness. These towns were later shared with the tribe of Simeon, whose territory sat inside Judah's borders.

Ziklag, Madmannah, and Sansannah were border towns in the far south. The Philistines held Ziklag until King Achish gave it to David while he was running from King Saul. From David's time on, Ziklag remained a possession of the kings of Judah.

This summary completes the southern list with Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon. The text counts twenty-nine cities here, even though thirty-eight names appear in total. Commentators explain that nine of these towns were soon transferred to the tribe of Simeon, or that only walled cities were counted in the official total.

The record turns to the rolling foothills called the Shephelah, a fertile region between the central mountains and the Mediterranean Sea. Eshtaol and Zorah were located here and later became famous as the homeland and burial place of Samson. These foothills gave Judah rich soil for farming as well as a natural barrier to protect against coastal invaders.

Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, and Azekah were fortified towns set among the valleys. Adullam was the area where David hid in a cave while running from Saul, choosing to stay close to his tribe's homeland. Socoh was famous as the site where David later defeated Goliath, the Philistine champion.

Shaaraim, Adithaim, and Gederah completed this first group of lowland settlements. The passage lists fourteen cities, though fifteen names are read, likely because Gederah and Gederothaim were two parts of the same town. God gave Judah this clear inventory so they would not lose their inheritance through fear or laziness.

Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad, Dilan, Mizpeh, and Joktheel open a second group of lowland towns further northwest. These settlements were scattered across the plains as farming and pasture communities. The name Joktheel means God nourishes or sustains, reminding the people of God's care over their daily life.

This passage completes sixteen lowland cities, including the powerful strongholds of Lachish and Eglon. Lachish was a major royal city, while Bozkath was the hometown of King Josiah's mother. Beth-dagon was named after the Philistine idol Dagon, showing that pagan worship once ruled places that now belonged to God's people.

Libnah, Ether, and Ashan begin a third group of lowland towns further south. Libnah was a fortified city that later rebelled against King Joram of Judah, while Ether was eventually given to the tribe of Simeon. God detailed each location so Judah would boldly step out to possess and guard what He gave them.
